did_you_know.text: The title “chief of the executioners” probably does not describe a kitchen cook, but a senior court official—perhaps the commander of the royal guard or executioners. The Hebrew word for “official” can also mean a court official, not necessarily a eunuch.
This chapter repeatedly presents Joseph as bringing blessing wherever he is. His success is not shown as merely personal; it also benefits the people around him.
The phrase “handsome in form and appearance” is a biblical formula for describing outward beauty. Similar wording appears in the description of Rachel and in other biblical stories.

Joseph sees loyalty to Potiphar as more than a social duty; he also calls the act “a sin against God.” The story therefore presents moral responsibility even when someone thinks no one will discover what they did.
The phrase “day after day” shows that this was not a one-time temptation, but repeated pressure. Joseph had to maintain a clear boundary consistently over time.

Here, “Hebrew” is used as a label for Joseph’s identity in the eyes of the Egyptians—a person from beyond the river or from another land. It describes an outsider, not a modern-style national identity.

The prison is described as a place for the king’s prisoners, so it may have been connected with the royal administration rather than serving only as an ordinary criminals’ jail. This setting helps explain how Joseph later encounters people from Pharaoh’s court.

The story emphasizes that Joseph can find favor and succeed even while imprisoned. This suggests an important idea: in the Bible, success does not always mean freedom or an easy life, but can also mean acting well within a difficult situation.
